notes.meaning: Here begins a summary of Israel's whole trip, from leaving Egypt to the edge of the promised land. The people did not wander off as a mob. They marched out in ordered groups, like an army with banners. Moses and Aaron led them as guides, serving under God.

other.label: Catholic and Orthodox
other.view: The early church writer Jerome wrote a study of these forty-two stopping places. He treated them as a picture of the Christian's journey from earth to heaven.

notes.meaning: God told Moses to keep a written record of the trip, like a travel diary. It helped prove the story was true and kept a memory of what God had done. It also built up the people's faith before they entered Canaan. The places are listed by where they set out from, which keeps the eye on where they were going. Christians, too, can find it helpful to write down God's care for them, because our memories easily forget.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars accept the list as accurate. But they think its neat pattern of about forty sites, one for each year, may show it was arranged to help people remember it. That could explain why some places are left out.

notes.meaning: Israel left Egypt the day after the Passover. They went out boldly, literally "with a high hand," because God's mighty hand was at work for them. They did not sneak away. The Egyptians, crushed by the death of their firstborn, had no power to stop them. God also judged Egypt's gods by showing they could not protect anyone. Some old writers think the idols were broken, while others think "gods" here may mean Egypt's rulers.
Succoth means "booths" or "tents." It may not have been a town at all. It was simply the first place the people set up their tents after leaving Rameses.

Etham stood at the edge of the wilderness. At first Israel camped only on the edge, and later deep in the desert. Matthew Henry sees God gently preparing his people for bigger hardships by giving them smaller ones first.

Israel turned back toward Pi-hahiroth because God commanded it (Exodus 14:2). It looked like going the wrong way, as if they were lost in a maze. Yet the pillar of cloud and fire was guiding them the whole time. God's way is always the best way, even when it does not seem the shortest.

In a few words, this verse recalls the great miracle of crossing through the sea. Then the people walked three days with no water, and God kept that huge crowd alive. At Marah they complained about the bitter water. Even so, God showed them mercy.

After the hard march, God brought his grumbling people to Elim, a pleasant oasis with twelve springs and seventy palm trees. Calvin sees this as a sign of God's amazing mercy. Some writers note that the list says nothing of the complaining at Marah but stops to mention Elim's water and trees. It encourages us to remember God's kindnesses.

This camp was by another part of the same sea they had crossed. It is mentioned nowhere else in the Bible. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown notes that the route fits the land very well, since this was the only practical road.
The Desert of Sin lies between Elim and Mount Sinai. Moses passes over it quickly here, yet it was a key place. There the people complained, and God sent manna, bread from heaven, to feed them.

Dophkah is not named in Exodus, and no one knows where it was. Exodus seems to skip it because nothing special happened there. Even so, it was a real stop for God's people on the way to the promised land.
Alush is also missing from Exodus, and its location is unknown. Old Jewish tradition, reported by John Gill, says Israel kept its first Sabbath (day of rest) here.

Rephidim is remembered because there was no water. The people turned against Moses, and God gave them water from the rock (Exodus 17). Naming the place was enough to bring the whole story to mind. In the same way, we should remember the times God has cared for us.
At the Wilderness of Sinai God gave his law and bound Israel to himself as his people. Calvin notes that soon after, they fell into worshiping a golden calf. That sin slowed their journey.

Kibroth-hattaavah means "graves of craving." The place was named for the plague that struck when the people grumbled and greedily demanded meat (Numbers 11). Its very name was a warning about God's judgment.
Hazeroth means "unwalled villages." It was the place where Miriam and Aaron spoke against Moses (Numbers 12).
Rithmah is named after the broom bush. Many commentators think it was the camp near Kadesh from which the twelve spies were sent into Canaan (Numbers 13).

From here on, most of the stops seem to belong to the long years of wandering after the people refused to enter Canaan. That was about thirty-eight years of discipline. Rimmon-perez itself is unknown.
No one is sure where Libnah was. Its name may mean "white." Like many of these stops, it was probably a desert camp that left no trace behind.
Rissah appears nowhere else in the Bible, and its location is unknown. During these years the camps seem to have been chosen near water and grass for the flocks.
Kehelathah may mean "assembly," but where it was is unknown. An old Jewish paraphrase of the Bible connects it with Korah's rebellion (Numbers 16).
No one can say where Mount Shepher was. Its name has been explained as "mount of beauty."
Haradah is unknown. The name may mean "frightening." One old suggestion places it near Kadesh.
Makheloth is found nowhere else in Scripture. Its name may mean "gatherings." Most places along this part of the journey cannot be found today.
Tahath is unknown. The name probably means "below." It may point to a camp lower down, perhaps on the way into a desert valley.
Terah is also unknown. Its name may mean "delay." It could mark a longer rest where there was better pasture.

Mithkah may mean "sweetness," perhaps of its water or grass. Calvin says this long list reminds Israel that their own stubbornness kept them wandering. Yet God still kept them and fed them. As Matthew Henry puts it, God led them about, yet led them the right way.
